title: "Reproducibility repositories"
subtitle: "From a licensed archive to preregistering your own reanalysis"
---

This is the repositories module of the [companion curriculum](index.qmd), and it is optional. Rather than tour research-data repositories in the abstract, it follows the actual trail this workshop's own data took: which archive holds the raw microdata behind the EU-frames case, why that microdata never enters this workshop's own materials, which OSF nodes the workshop fetches from and why, and how a preregistration – yours, the Multi100 team's, or the facilitator's own follow-up article – gets written down before an analysis runs. By the end, the module adds a section on preregistration templates that feeds directly into Block 3 of the workshop day, where you complete one yourself.

The module assumes no more than the workshop itself does. You do not need to have taken [the git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd) first, though the two are natural companions: this module is mostly about other people's materials and about a study plan you commit to in writing; the git and GitHub module is about the tool, git, that lets you keep a record of how your own materials changed over time.

## 1. GESIS: a licensed archive, and why the raw data never travels with this workshop {#sec-gesis}

The EU-frames case rests on sixteen waves of Eurobarometer survey data, and Eurobarometer's German distributor is **GESIS – Leibniz Institute for the Social Sciences**, which describes itself as "[the largest German infrastructure institute for the social sciences](https://www.gesis.org/en/institute)". It runs Germany's central social-science data archive, holding more than seven thousand studies, certified to the CoreTrustSeal standard and organised around the FAIR principles (findable, accessible, interoperable, reusable). This is the institutionally-managed kind of repository: not a general-purpose deposit box that accepts anything from anyone, but an archive run by a funded body that curates a named collection under its own terms.

Those terms are the reason this workshop's own repository looks the way it does. GESIS's licence for the Eurobarometer scientific-use files does not permit redistributing the raw microdata, so the two datasets this workshop actually ships – `rep_data.csv` and `EUframes_cy.csv` – are not the microdata itself but **derived country-year aggregates**, built once from the raw files and then released under their own, more permissive terms (CC BY 4.0 for the derived data; the codebook states this explicitly). The preparation scripts that built them are kept in the template repository as an **exhibit**: code you can read to see exactly how the aggregates were constructed, not a pipeline you can point at a folder of raw files, because no raw files are there to point at. This is the same "commit only what the licence allows" discipline that governs any project built on licensed survey data, and it is worth naming plainly rather than leaving as an unstated background fact: a workshop that redistributed the raw microdata, even to a closed group of participants, would be breaching the terms under which GESIS makes the data available in the first place.

If you want the raw data yourself – to check the aggregation, to try a person-level specification the country-year files cannot support, or simply because a licensed archive is worth learning to use – the route is a free registration with GESIS at [search.gesis.org](https://search.gesis.org/), followed by GESIS's own request process for the specific Eurobarometer waves the codebook names. This is precisely the tiered-access pattern common to institutional archives: viewing a catalogue entry is open to everyone, but obtaining the file itself means registering under your own name and agreeing to the archive's conditions. Registering is a normal step in a working researcher's life, not a barrier put up to be difficult, and it is the reason the analyst who originally built this claim, the Multi100 team who reanalysed it, and this workshop's own corrected rebuild could all work from the same sixteen waves without any of them ever redistributing a byte of GESIS data to the other.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Open the [data codebook](../data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md) and read its final section, "Licence". Write one sentence distinguishing what is licensed under CC BY 4.0 from what remains subject to GESIS terms, and one sentence on what a "derived aggregate" is doing in that distinction – why summarising sixteen waves down to one row per country-year changes what you are allowed to share, even though the underlying facts are the same.
:::

## 2. The OSF constellation: this paper's own trail {#sec-osf}

The **Open Science Framework** (OSF), run by the non-profit Center for Open Science, is the general-purpose repository behind almost everything else this workshop touches. Its help pages describe an OSF **project** as "[a flexible, collaborative workspace where researchers can plan, manage, and share any part of their research lifecycle](https://help.osf.io/article/253-project-structure)", and a **component** as an "[optional sub-project nested within a parent project ... used to break a large project into smaller parts](https://help.osf.io/article/253-project-structure)". Projects and components form a parent–child tree, and each node can carry files, a wiki, contributors and its own privacy setting. That structure is the map to read for the EU-frames case, and three nodes matter for this workshop specifically.

**`osf.io/8rtwe` – the official Multi100 archival record.** This is the component the Multi100 project itself preserved for analyst C6HJR: the materials as originally submitted, uncorrected, including a data-preparation error that the workshop tells as an open story in its Block 2 ([the git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd#sec-why) recounts it in full). It is the archival record in the strict sense – frozen, citable, unchanged since deposit.

**`osf.io/6zqct` – the analyst's maintained fork, and the workshop's own fetch target.** OSF describes this node itself as "a public fork" of `8rtwe`, maintained by the facilitator for educational purposes, and it holds two folders: `moreh_rep/`, an exact copy of the as-submitted materials (including `rep_data.csv`, byte-identical to the published file, giving t = −3.853 under the constrained model), and `moreh_rep_vAPR2025/`, the corrected version. That second folder is where the analyst's own annotated correction lives – the script comment quoted and discussed in the git and GitHub module – along with revised Task 1 and Task 2 documents. This is the node every fetch in this workshop actually targets, precisely because it carries both the original error and its documented fix, side by side, rather than only the tidied-up final state.

**`osf.io/h7432` – the full SCORE dossier, one paper put through all three Rs.** This is the parent node under which the whole reproducibility apparatus around the EU-frames case sits, and reading its component table is the clearest way to see a repository trail do real evidentiary work.

| Component | What | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| `whp4b` | Original materials collected by the Center for Open Science | View-only |
| `cf8en` | Author-provided code – two Stata do-files, supplied on request; the author's own statement records that the data cannot be forwarded and must come from GESIS | Code available, data restricted |
| `8fwrt` | Power analysis for the replication | – |
| `ezhcs` | **Push-button reproduction**, run with the author's own code | **Failed.** "The authors used file names that did not correspond with the names of the files available for download. Additionally 16 datasets are listed on the website as being used but the code references 18 files." |
| `4rjbf` | **Source-data reproduction** | **'Not reproduced'** – the effect size "could not be extract[ed] nor re-calculate[d]" from the source data |
| `gr8u6` | **Multi100 robustness** – five independent reanalysts, including analyst C6HJR whose materials this workshop reanalyses | All five coefficients negative (claim-consistent direction); partial r ranging from −0.006 to −0.452, a span of two orders of magnitude |
| `zt5y2` | **Secondary-data replication** – fresh Eurobarometer and Eurostat waves, preregistered, N = 352,114 person-year observations | **Not replicated – sign flip.** "We found a positive coefficient for unemployment on cosmopolitan framing": b = +0.002, p = .046 |

Reading down that table is a worked lesson in what a well-kept repository trail lets a reader establish without emailing anyone. The push-button check failed for a mundane, checkable reason – file names that did not match what was actually available for download – not because the underlying claim was wrong. The source-data check failed differently: the code ran, but the reported effect size could not be recovered from it. The robustness check, the one this workshop stands inside, held the claim's direction across five independent analysts while the effect size itself moved by a factor of roughly 75. And the replication, run on genuinely new data under a preregistered plan, flipped sign entirely. One paper, three different verdicts on three different questions – reproduction, robustness, replicability – each one legible only because the materials behind it sit in a public, node-by-node OSF tree rather than in a folder on someone's laptop.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Open [`osf.io/h7432`](https://osf.io/h7432/) and find the `zt5y2` component from the table above. Locate the sentence reporting the sign-flipped coefficient in the component's own materials, and note the exact figures: the coefficient, its standard error, and the significance level. This is the same scavenger task the in-session OSF segment sets in Block 3 – if you are working through this module before the workshop, you will already know where to look when it comes up.
:::

## 3. What "registration" and "fork" mean on OSF, and where the companion article's own registration stands {#sec-registration}

Two pieces of OSF vocabulary complete the foundation for the rest of this module. A **registration** is "[a frozen version of your project that can never be edited or deleted, but you can issue a withdrawal of it later](https://help.osf.io/article/330-registrations)", time-stamped and given its own permanent identifier. This is the mechanism behind preregistration: it captures a study plan before the data are seen (or, for a reanalysis of existing data, before the specific analytical choices are made), so the plan cannot later be quietly rewritten to fit the result. The Multi100 team's own reanalysts worked from exactly this kind of frozen, dated protocol, which is one reason their five independent results can be compared on equal footing.

A **fork**, discussed in [the git and GitHub module](git-github.qmd#sec-github) in its git and GitHub sense, has a direct OSF equivalent: your own editable copy of a public node, kept separate from the original so you can change it without touching that original's record. `osf.io/6zqct` is precisely this – OSF's own description of it as "a public fork" of `8rtwe` is not a loose figure of speech but the platform's own term for the manoeuvre.

The facilitator's own current project puts both pieces of vocabulary to use at once. A companion journal article – extending this workshop's case into a fuller multiverse, with a person-level analysis grid and a combined "joint universe" of specifications alongside the country-year analysis you work with here – has a preregistration that is **drafted, to be registered**: written, but not yet filed as an OSF registration at the time of writing. This matters for how the workshop's Block 4 discussion of that article is framed. Nothing computed under that drafted plan appears anywhere in this workshop's materials yet, and nothing will, until the registration is actually filed and the analyses it describes are run – that sequencing (plan first, filed and frozen; computation second, only afterwards) is the entire point of the registration mechanism just described, and skipping it would undermine the very thing the article sets out to demonstrate. What the drafted plan does already establish, because it extends analysis already completed on the same 840-specification grid you use in Block 4, is a decomposition of how much each analytical choice moves the result: the outcome variable you choose – which of the four framing scales, or their composites – accounts for roughly half of all the variation across the grid, dwarfing the choice of estimator, predictor form, co-predictor or weighting scheme combined. The plan for what comes next, once filed, adds a person-level grid of 3,840 specifications, a joint universe of 5,520 combining both levels, and a formal curve-level permutation test (500 iterations, refitting the 840 aggregated Gaussian specifications) asking not just how the specifications spread out but whether that spread is more than chance would produce. You will hear this framed in Block 4 as work in progress rather than as a finished result, because at the time of the workshop that is exactly what it is.

## 4. Preregistration templates: from the simplest form to a plan built for existing data {#sec-prereg-templates}

Everything so far in this module has been about reading other people's registrations. This closing section turns to writing your own, because Block 3 of the workshop asks you to do exactly that – complete a preregistration template block in your own report, before you run your chosen specification.

An **OSF registration**, as defined above, is the general mechanism: a frozen, time-stamped, permanent copy of a study plan. What varies between registrations is the **template** used to structure that plan – the specific set of questions a researcher answers before the data are touched. OSF hosts several, built for different kinds of study, and two are worth knowing by name.

**The AsPredicted-style short template.** Originally built by the team behind [AsPredicted.org](https://aspredicted.org/) and available as one of OSF's own built-in registration forms, this is the simplest entry point into preregistration and the one recommended for the in-session exercise. It asks a short, fixed sequence of questions – what the hypotheses are, what the key variables and analysis are, how the sample will be determined, and what would count as excluding data – each answered in a sentence or two rather than a full protocol document. Its appeal for a workshop setting is exactly its brevity: a participant with no prior preregistration experience can complete it in the time Block 3 sets aside, and the discipline it enforces (state the analysis before running it, in a form specific enough that it cannot be quietly reinterpreted afterwards) is the same discipline a longer template enforces, just asked in fewer words.

**The secondary-data preregistration template (van den Akker and colleagues).** A short-form template written for a fresh, not-yet-collected study assumes something that is not true of this workshop's exercise: that the researcher has not yet seen the data. A reanalysis of an existing, already-public dataset like the Eurobarometer country-year panel breaks that assumption from the outset – you can see summary statistics, published tables, even other researchers' results, before you commit to a specification of your own. Van den Akker and colleagues' template is built around that difference. Where a fresh-data template asks what you will collect and how, a secondary-data template asks what you have already seen and what you have not: which parts of the dataset or its published results you have already been exposed to, whether your hypothesis was formed before or after that exposure, and what remains genuinely undetermined about your specific analytical choices at the point of writing the plan. For a Multi100-style robustness reanalysis – exactly the kind of exercise this workshop runs – this is the more accurate match for what preregistration can actually promise: not that you approached the data blind, which would rarely be true of a reanalysis, but that your specific analytical path was fixed and dated before you ran the numbers down it.

**How the workshop's own template block maps onto these.** The report skeleton you complete in Block 3 is modelled on the AsPredicted-style short form's structure – a small number of short, specific questions rather than a full protocol – but adapted for a specification-menu reanalysis rather than a fresh study: instead of "what is your hypothesis and how will you test it", the block asks you to state your chosen specification (one option from each of the eight menu axes) and to justify that choice against the estimand and DAG you built earlier in the day. This is deliberately the lighter of the two templates, chosen because Block 3's time budget favours a form participants can complete and render inside a defined slot rather than one that demands a fuller protocol. The secondary-data template is signposted as pre-session and take-home reading rather than completed live, for anyone who wants to see how the same discipline scales up to a plan detailed enough to submit as a real OSF registration – which is, after all, the form the facilitator's own companion-article preregistration in section 3 above eventually needs to take.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Try it

Read the AsPredicted template's question list at [aspredicted.org](https://aspredicted.org/) and, separately, skim the secondary-data template's structure. For a single specification you might choose from the [specification menu](../exercise/spec-menu.qmd) – say, outcome = `mpos`, predictor form = raw `unemp`, two-way fixed effects, all years, no weights – write one sentence answering the secondary-data template's central question in your own words: what, if anything, had you already seen about this claim's results before settling on that specification? A truthful answer to that question, written down before anything runs, is what separates a preregistration that constrains you from one that only decorates a result you had already half-decided on.
:::

## Sources and attribution {#sec-sources}

The definitional material in this module – what a DOI is, what an OSF project, component and registration are, what a fork means on OSF – draws on the same primary sources as the trust-multilab companion curriculum's own repositories module: the OSF help pages (<https://help.osf.io>), quoted directly and linked in place wherever they appear above. The GESIS self-description in section 1 is likewise a direct quotation from the institute's own site (<https://www.gesis.org/en/institute>). None of this definitional material is workshop-specific; it describes the platforms themselves, so the same quotations hold regardless of which project's data trail is being followed.

Everything else – the GESIS licensing constraint on this workshop's own data, the three-node OSF trail (`8rtwe`, `6zqct`, `h7432`) and its component table, the companion article's registration status, and the mapping from the workshop's own template block onto the AsPredicted-style and secondary-data templates – is this workshop's own worked example, drawn from the [data codebook](../data/EUframes_cy_codebook.md), the OSF nodes themselves, and the facilitator's own project notes. Direct quotations from the OSF dossier's component reports (`ezhcs`, `4rjbf`, `zt5y2`) are reproduced exactly as they appear in those components' own materials.

For the version-control half of taking a reanalysis further – putting your own report, and eventually your own registration, under a history you can read and correct – see [the git and GitHub module, Git and GitHub for reproducible research](git-github.qmd).
